N001 and real-order approximation from either side of 1 prove the exact equality. No limit is interchanged with a sum or infimum.

background_notes.fact: For q>0, N^(-q)→0 through positive integers N; also 1/N→0. In S001 q=a-1>0, so the equal-interval covers eventually have diameter at most any fixed delta>0 and a-cost below any fixed eta>0.

grounds.reason: a>1, N is a positive integer, and the displayed mesh and cost are 1/N and N^(1-a).

background_notes.justification: Real powers on positive numbers are defined by exp(r log x), giving the usual monotonicity and inverse identities. Given delta,eta>0, choose an integer N larger than both 1/delta and eta^(-1/q). The stated bounds follow. Thus every fixed-scale infimum is zero; its supremum over scales is zero.

background_notes.fact: Every nonempty subset V of R of finite diameter rho is bounded, has real endpoints l=inf V and u=sup V, and u-l=rho. For every h>0 the interval (l-h,u+h) contains V and has length rho+2h. A countable family can be enumerated with empty padding, and its nonempty indices form a countable subset of N.

grounds.reason: Under L1 each nonempty V_i has diameter rho_i≤delta<infinity; epsilon>0 gives h=epsilon 2^(-i-2)>0.
Diameter is the supremum of pairwise distances.
Lebesgue measure of an open interval is its length.

background_notes.justification: For a fixed v in V, all points lie in [v-rho,v+rho]. Real completeness gives l,u. Every pairwise distance is at most u-l, while points approaching the infimum and supremum have distances approaching u-l; hence the diameter equals u-l. Strict enlargement then gives containment and the displayed length. Countability permits an enumeration, padding finite lists by empty sets; deleting empty members does not alter the union or positive-exponent cost. These are routine facts for the actual intervals constructed in S002.

background_notes.fact: Measures, including lambda, are monotone and have the function-like outer-measure structure required by M005. For nonnegative countable families, sums preserve inequalities and split over addition; for T⊆N, sum_{i in T}2^(-i-1)≤1. Consequently sum_{i in T}(rho_i+epsilon 2^(-i-1))≤sum_{i in T}rho_i+epsilon. For fixed C in [0,infinity], if 1≤C+epsilon for every real epsilon>0, then C≥1.

grounds.reason: lambda is the standard Lebesgue measure.
T⊆N, rho_i≥0, epsilon>0, and I⊆union J_i.
V,T,rho remain independent of epsilon; M005 supplies the countable union bound.

background_notes.justification: Countable additivity on disjoint sets yields monotonicity by splitting B as A and B\A, and yields the outer-measure union inequality by disjointification; thus a measure satisfies the structure stipulated by M005. Nonnegative series are suprema of finite partial sums, so comparison and addition follow by finite sums and cofinal finite unions. The geometric partial sums of 2^(-i-1), starting at i=0, are 1-2^(-m), with supremum 1; a subseries is no larger. If C is finite and C<1, choosing epsilon=(1-C)/2 contradicts 1≤C+epsilon; the infinite case already satisfies C≥1.

background_notes.fact: For fixed finite c>0 and nonnegative terms x_i,y_i, x_i≥c y_i for every i implies sum_i x_i≥c sum_i y_i, with the usual extended nonnegative interpretation. If every admissible cover cost is at least b, its infimum is at least b. If H_delta is unbounded over positive delta, sup_{delta>0}H_delta=infinity.

grounds.reason: c=delta^(s-1) is finite positive; x_i=rho_i^s, y_i=rho_i, and F003 gives sum_i y_i≥1.
H^s_delta is the infimum over cover costs and H^s the supremum over positive scales.

background_notes.justification: Finite-sum comparison followed by the supremum over finite subsets proves the series inequality; multiplication by a fixed positive finite constant commutes with that supremum, including an infinite value. The infimum statement is the defining greatest-lower-bound property (also valid for an empty family); the supremum statement is its corresponding least-upper-bound property. These justify the existing cover-to-content and content-to-measure steps.

background_notes.fact: For d in [0,infinity], bounds d≤a for every real a>1 and d≥s for every real 0<s<1 imply d=1.

grounds.reason: N001 and the equal-interval covers give d=dimH(I)≤a for every a>1.
N001 and the divergent lower costs give d≥s for every s in (0,1).

background_notes.justification: The upper bounds imply d is finite, for example d≤2. If d>1, choose a=(1+d)/2, contradicting d≤a. If 0≤d<1, choose s=(1+d)/2, contradicting d≥s. Hence both d≤1 and d≥1 hold, exactly as S001 and S005 conclude.

background_notes.fact: For 0<s<1 and 0<x≤d with d>0, x^(s-1)≥d^(s-1), so x^s≥d^(s-1)x. For x=0 both sides of the latter inequality are zero. Also d^(s-1) is unbounded as d>0 decreases to zero.

grounds.reason: s is fixed in (0,1), delta>0, and under L1 every rho_i lies in [0,delta].
The proof separates rho_i=0 from rho_i>0 before dividing by rho_i.

background_notes.justification: Writing q=1-s>0 gives x^(s-1)=1/x^q. Positive powers are increasing, so reciprocals give the required reversed inequality. Positive-exponent powers at zero are zero. For every M>0, choosing 0<d<M^(-1/q) gives d^(s-1)>M, which justifies the later unbounded-scale conclusion without a limit exchange.
